content: The development of the WHO guideline on the use of safety-engineered syringes in healthcare settings involved a rigorous and collaborative process. All decisions, including the final recommendations and accompanying statements, were reached through consensus among the Guideline Development Group (GDG) members. The GDG unanimously agreed on the recommendations and all related statements. Based on discussions during the GDG meeting, as well as evidence from GRADE tables and recommendations developed during the meeting, a draft of the full guideline document was prepared by the Technical Focal Point on Injection Safety within the SDS Department. This draft was shared with the WHO Steering Committee, other WHO departments at headquarters, regional injection safety focal points, and the GDG for review. Subsequently, the draft underwent external peer review. A group of external experts was consulted to provide input on the scope of the guideline, the questions addressed, the selection of important outcomes for decision-making, and to review the completed draft. This group included key WHO partners, country development partners, major health program funders, injection safety and infection control focal points, professional associations, patient associations, infection control societies, NGOs, and major injection device manufacturers (contacted as observers through the Global Medical Technology Alliance). The consultation was conducted via email with selected experts known for their experience in injection safety and through the SIGN Post List Serve, an electronic weekly newsletter with over 1,500 subscribers. The external experts expressed significant interest in the new policy guidance and provided valuable comments, which were incorporated into the final version of the guideline. These comments were cataloged and addressed in the final drafts presented to support the GDG meeting. External reviewers who contributed were acknowledged in the guideline. In accordance with WHO rules, all experts participating in the guideline development process were required to declare any relevant interests prior to their involvement. GDG members completed a Declaration of Interests form before the group composition and invitations were finalized. Procedures for managing conflicts of interest were followed in line with WHO guidelines. All GDG members declared that they had no commercial, financial, or personal interests directly or indirectly related to the topic of the guideline. The guideline includes specific recommendations for the use of safety-engineered syringes. For syringes with sharps injury protection (SIP) features, the recommendation is conditional, based on moderate-quality evidence. A systematic review concluded that SIP devices reduce the incidence of needlestick injuries (NSIs) among healthcare workers (HCWs) and patients. While the evidence was of moderate quality, the benefits were judged to outweigh the risks. Preliminary results from a WHO cost-effectiveness study support this recommendation. In settings where SIP devices are introduced, it is estimated that nine fewer HCWs per 1,000 would experience an NSI over one year, with no expected harms. Greater benefits are anticipated in areas with higher prevalence of HIV, HBV, and HCV or higher rates of sharps injuries. For syringes with re-use prevention (RUP) features, the recommendation is also conditional, based on very low-quality evidence. Evidence from a systematic review supports the use of RUP syringes to reduce re-use and associated disease transmission. Although the evidence is limited, the benefits are likely to outweigh the risks. Cost-effectiveness studies coordinated by WHO indicate that the introduction of RUP devices is cost-effective. In settings where RUP devices have been introduced, reductions in syringe re-use have been documented, leading to fewer diseases transmitted through unsafe injection practices. No harms are expected, and greater benefits are anticipated in areas with higher disease prevalence or higher re-use rates. The implementation of safety-engineered syringes should be part of a comprehensive approach that includes education and training, surveillance, reporting and management of NSIs, post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP), involvement of frontline workers in device selection, immunization of HCWs against HBV, advocacy for standard precautions, and monitoring and evaluation of the strategy's impact. The estimated costs of implementation should account for all components of this comprehensive approach, as well as the cost of the devices themselves. The GDG identified several areas for future research, including effectiveness studies in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), research on the burden of diseases associated with syringe re-use and NSIs, cost-effectiveness studies, and better integration of RUP and SIP features into a single device. Specific research needs for SIP devices include updating the global burden of disease from NSIs, studying attitudes and practices related to NSI reporting and PEP use, re-evaluating the risk of bloodborne virus transmission following NSIs, and assessing the impact of SIP introduction on waste disposal and recycling. The guideline emphasizes the importance of dissemination, adaptation, and implementation to improve the quality and safety of care and health outcomes related to injection practices. WHO has developed a global campaign to promote injection safety, which includes advocacy, information, and communication efforts. The guideline will be translated into all official UN languages and disseminated electronically through WHO websites, CD-ROMs, and slide presentations. A summary brochure will also be produced to enhance dissemination and serve as an advocacy tool for decision-makers.
